archetype.name: Pretender (record ahead of its play)
archetype.definition: A team whose .500-plus start rests on finishing and a few close wins while it is outshot and out-chanced nearly every night, so the record is likely to sink toward its underlying level.

report.headline: A winning-looking record built on hot finishing over last-place shot share
report.take:
Seattle sits 9-8-1, fourth in the Pacific, with a 19-point start that paces to 87 points. That makes it look like a bubble team. The site ranks it 29th of 32, and the underlying numbers back the site, not the standings. The Kraken own the league's worst 5-on-5 shot-attempt share (CF % 41%) and the 30th-ranked expected-goals share (43.3%). They take 24.2 shots a game (30th) and allow 30.4 (29th). Every roster group grades in the D range: D+ forwards, D+ blueline, D in goal. This is not a good team running into bad luck. It is a poor possession team that has been lucky in a specific way.

The luck is in the finishing. Seattle's skaters shoot 12.6% in all situations, sixth in the league and well above the 11.4% average, and the 5-on-5 PDO is 103. That is how a team near the bottom in shots still scores 3.28 goals a game (13th). Freddy Gaudreau's 8 goals on 21 shots is the clearest example. Defense has given nothing back. Seattle allows 3.67 a game (29th), the penalty kill is 31st at 62.7%, and opposing forwards score well above their norms, with wingers taking an outsized share of the points against. The Pts vs Goal Diff figure (+1) says close games have been only slightly kind, so the record mostly mirrors the goals. The goals themselves are the part flattered by shooting.

The correction has already started. October was a .500-plus month with goals at 3.71 a game in both directions. Since then the shooting has cooled, and the last five games went 1-4 with 1.8 goals scored and 4.0 allowed. The ten-game stretch is 4-6 with a -16 differential. Once the finishing stops covering the shot deficit, this is what the team looks like.

History points the same way. Last season's 79-point team had a 45% CF and 46% xGF, and this year's possession is worse on both. The bright spots are real but narrow. Berkly Catton is the only regular forward above 50% in expected goals (53.7%) and leads the group in Game Score. Philipp Grubauer has been roughly average (-0.2 GSAx) while Joey Daccord has struggled (.872, -3.6). Neither is enough to hold a playoff line on 41% of the shot attempts.

strengths.title: Finishing well above league rate
strengths.body: Seattle converts 12.6% of its shots, sixth in the league, and that keeps scoring mid-pack despite one of the lowest shot volumes. Gaudreau, Samoskevich and Eberle have all finished well. Some of it is skill, but a rate this far above average on so few shots is the most regression-prone number on the sheet.

strengths.title: Catton's line tilts the ice
strengths.body: Berkly Catton is the one regular forward who wins his minutes. He posts a 53.7% xGF with 14 points and the forward group's best Game Score. In a lineup where almost everyone else sits around or below 45%, his line is the only one generating more than it allows, and that looks sustainable.

strengths.title: Grubauer has held his own
strengths.body: Philipp Grubauer has been close to average: a .893 save % and -0.2 GSAx behind a team that bleeds shots. Joey Daccord's .872 and -3.6 account for most of the team's negative goaltending number. Leaning on Grubauer is the quickest lever the club has.

concerns.title: Outshot and out-chanced nightly
concerns.body: Seattle is last in the league in CF % and 30th in xGF %, 9 points of shot share below average. It also allows more shots than it takes by a wide margin. Shot share stabilizes quickly and was already poor last season, so this is the team's true level rather than an early blip.

concerns.title: A penalty kill that fails often
concerns.body: The PK has killed just 62.7% of penalties, 31st, and 14.7 points below the league average. The skaters have allowed shots in bulk and the goaltending hasn't bailed them out shorthanded. Kills usually drift back toward average, but last season's 72.2% was already below league level, so a full recovery isn't a given.

concerns.title: The offense has already cooled
concerns.body: Over the last five games Seattle scored 1.8 a game, 1.48 below its season rate, and went 1-4. November's scoring has roughly halved October's. With a 5-on-5 PDO of 103 and few shots, the early goal rate was always borrowed, and this looks like the bill arriving rather than a slump that simply ends.

trend.note: October's even-goals, winning month gave way to a November where scoring collapsed. The last five games produced one win and a -11 differential.

weekAhead.headline: Two soft opponents, then Anaheim's power play tests the kill
weekAhead.body:
The schedule eases. Vancouver comes to Seattle at 4-17-1 and last on the site, with the league's worst save % (.862), worst Goalies GSAx and worst defense against forwards. San Jose (10-11-2) shoots poorly but has a B+ goaltending group, the kind that can blunt Seattle's finishing on the road. Anaheim (11-9-1) then visits with a strong offense and an F-graded goaltending group.

For a team that just went 1-4, this is the right week to stop the bleeding. Two home games against porous goaltending give the shooters a chance to score again without needing more shots. The danger is Seattle's habit of giving up volume, which matters least against Vancouver and most against an Anaheim team that finishes well and scores on the power play at the league's best rate. Taking two of three would be par, and anything less would confirm how far the slide has gone.

keyMatchups.title: Seattle PK vs Anaheim's power play
keyMatchups.body: Anaheim's power play converts 35.2%, first in the league, and Seattle's kill ranks 31st. Every Kraken penalty on Nov. 23 is close to a coin flip. Staying out of the box is the clearest path to a home win.

keyMatchups.title: Vancouver's goaltending as a reset
keyMatchups.body: The Canucks' goalies are last in save % (.862) and Goalies GSAx (-13.7), and their defense is the worst against forwards. A Seattle offense managing 1.8 goals a game lately should find goals here even on modest shot totals.

keyMatchups.title: Sharks' goalies vs Seattle's shooters
keyMatchups.body: San Jose's goalies are sixth in GSAx (9.5). That is the one strength on a 27th-ranked goal-differential team. Seattle relies on shooting % rather than volume, so a hot goalie on the road is the week's likeliest loss.

weekAhead.watch: Whether Seattle wins the shot count against Vancouver. If it can't outshoot the league's 32nd-ranked team, the possession problem has no easy fix.

restOfSeason.body:
The 87-point pace is the ceiling, not the forecast. Seattle's goal totals are propped up by a sixth-ranked shooting % and a 103 PDO. The process underneath is last in shot attempts and 30th in expected goals, worse than last season's 79-point team. As finishing drifts toward league average, scoring should settle below three a game, and the defense has no sign of tightening. A modest rebound in the penalty kill and more starts for Grubauer could offset part of that. I expect a final total in the mid-to-high 70s in points, about where the last two seasons landed, and well outside the playoff picture.

What would change that is real improvement in shot share. Catton's line shows it is possible, but one line can't carry a lineup where the top-minute defensemen and most forwards sit in the low 40s in xGF %. Absent that, the climb in the Pacific standings is likely to run in reverse.

confidence.note: 18 games is small, but the shot-share data is stable and matches last season's decline.
